nodes.name: Non-verbal behaviors underexplored
nodes.description: Existing studies mainly focus on simulating human dialogue; non-verbal behaviors like item clicking in recommender systems, though implicitly exhibiting user preferences, have not been deeply explored.

nodes.name: Gap between language and behavior modeling
nodes.description: The gap between universal language modeling and personalized behavior modeling, plus LLMs' incomprehension of user-item relations, is a main reason non-verbal behaviors are underexplored.

nodes.name: Verbalized interaction text fails to capture patterns
nodes.description: Verbalizing interaction records into natural language text to prompt LLMs struggles to capture underlying behavioral patterns, since semantically unrelated items (e.g., diapers and beer) can be behaviorally correlated in ways that confuse LLMs.

nodes.name: Item-side modeling neglected in prior work
nodes.description: Prior agent-based recommendation studies (e.g., RecAgent) mainly characterize user-side behaviors using universal LLMs, neglecting the effect of item-side modeling in the two-sided interaction process.

nodes.name: AgentCF proposal
nodes.description: AgentCF is proposed as an agent-based collaborative filtering approach that considers both users and items as agents, collaboratively optimized together, inspired by collaborative learning in traditional recommenders like BPR and NCF.

nodes.name: User and item memory modules
nodes.description: Both user and item agents are equipped with memory modules maintaining simulated preferences and tastes, including intrinsic features and acquired behavioral information.

nodes.name: User short-term and long-term memory
nodes.description: User agents are equipped with short-term memory (recently updated preference text) and long-term memory (a pool of historical preference texts) to reflect dynamically changing preferences.

nodes.name: Item unified memory
nodes.description: Item agents are equipped with a single unified memory module recording their characteristics and adopter preferences, since item information is relatively stable through time.

nodes.name: Autonomous interaction for contrastive item selection
nodes.description: User agents are presented with a contrastive pair of a positive and negative item candidate and tasked with selecting an item and providing an explanation, analogous to the forward computation of models like BPR.

nodes.name: Popularity and position bias introduced
nodes.description: To increase discrimination difficulty, a negative item with high popularity is sampled and placed before the positive item in the selection list, deliberately introducing popularity and position bias.

nodes.name: Collaborative reflection mechanism
nodes.description: Based on the disparity between an agent's decision and real-world interaction records, user and item agents are prompted to reflect on and adjust their memories in a mutual manner, serving as the 'backward update' analogous to gradient-based learning.

nodes.name: Negative item agent memory not modified
nodes.description: The memory of the negative item agent is not modified during reflection, because LLMs tend to over-complain about the negative item's drawbacks despite it possibly being attractive to other users.

nodes.name: Implicit preference propagation
nodes.description: Because memory of both user and item agents is updated for each interaction record, item memory becomes injected with adopter preferences, which propagate to subsequent users interacting with that item (and vice versa for users), implicitly modeling collaborative filtering.

nodes.name: Analogy to classical recommendation models
nodes.description: User and item memories serve as language-based parameters (embeddings); the selection process corresponds to forward preference evaluation and collaborative reflection corresponds to backward parameter update, with reflection acting as a 'semantic gradient'.

nodes.name: AgentCF outperforms baselines in most scenarios
nodes.description: AgentCF outperforms other baselines in most scenarios, highlighting the effectiveness of collaborative learning for simulating personalized agents.

nodes.name: AgentCF-B demonstrates preference propagation efficacy
nodes.description: The performance of the basic AgentCF-B variant, acting as a collaborative filtering recommender, demonstrates the efficacy of preference propagation in modeling the collaborative filtering idea.

nodes.name: AgentCF-B+R improves personalization
nodes.description: Retrieving user agents' specialized preferences toward candidates (AgentCF-B+R) enables more personalized inferences.

nodes.name: AgentCF-B+H better on sparse data
nodes.description: In sparse interaction cases (Office dataset), incorporating user historical interactions to enable LLMs as sequential recommenders (AgentCF-B+H) achieves better performance.

nodes.name: AgentCF comparable to full-dataset traditional recommenders
nodes.description: AgentCF achieves comparable performance to traditional recommenders trained on full datasets in sparse scenarios, despite being trained on only ~0.07% of the complete dataset.

nodes.name: Tuning-free baselines underperform
nodes.description: Existing tuning-free methods (Pop, BM25, LLMRank) exhibit unsatisfactory performance, with LLMRank falling significantly behind traditional models despite using ChatGPT with user historical interactions.

nodes.name: Removing autonomous interaction degrades performance
nodes.description: Without autonomous interaction (directly providing real interaction records to agents), performance drops, showing that comparing autonomous interactions to real-world records generates more comprehensive feedback for reflection.

nodes.name: Removing user agent optimization degrades performance
nodes.description: Without user agent memory updates (representing users by raw historical interactions), performance declines, showing simple verbalized interaction text cannot reflect underlying user preferences.

nodes.name: Removing item agent optimization degrades performance
nodes.description: Without item agent optimization (representing items by identity information only), performance also declines, highlighting the effectiveness of behavior-involved item-side modeling for capturing two-sided relations.

nodes.name: LLMRank susceptible to popularity/position bias
nodes.description: An LLM prompted by user historical interactions (LLMRank) is influenced by both popularity bias and position bias, tending to select popular and higher-positioned items.

nodes.name: AgentCF shows enhanced stability against bias
nodes.description: AgentCF, although inevitably affected by popularity and position bias, performs with enhanced stability compared to LLMRank, confirming it ranks candidates based on personalized preferences rather than general knowledge alone.

nodes.name: Continuous optimization improves agent-user alignment
nodes.description: Continuous optimization across steps enables user agents to align their preferences with real users, leading to an increasing number making correct choices on initial attempts before optimization at each step.

nodes.name: High post-reflection accuracy
nodes.description: Around 95% of user agents can make correct choices after collaborative reflection, highlighting its effectiveness.

nodes.name: User-user interaction via reviews
nodes.description: User agents can read and write reviews about items, simulating user-user social behaviors where test users read reviews from other user agents before deciding.

nodes.name: Simulated agents behave like real users toward reviews
nodes.description: Simulated user agents show a growing inclination to purchase items after positive reviews, refrain from purchasing after negative reviews, and trust reviews from users with similar preferences, akin to real-user behavior.

nodes.name: Item-item interaction alleviates cold-start
nodes.description: New item agents are prompted to interact with and learn from popular item agents with extensive interaction records, warming up cold-start items by estimating adopter preferences.

nodes.name: Item-item interaction improves ranking performance
nodes.description: The item-item interaction process enhances propagation of collected user preferences to new items and improves their ranking performance compared to using cold-start memory alone.

nodes.name: Dissimilar item interactions also help
nodes.description: Even interactions with item agents that differ in identity information can alleviate the cold-start problem to some extent, implying new item agents comprehend the relationship between identity information and personalized memory rather than simply replicating other agents' memories.

nodes.name: Seed preference propagation experiment
nodes.description: A seed user agent is initialized with special preference descriptions not spontaneously emerging during normal optimization, then agents autonomously interact and optimize memories to observe propagation.

nodes.name: Propagation increases then decays with scope
nodes.description: Through continuous interactions, an increasing number of user agents with similar behaviors to the seed user express similar preferences, but the proportion gradually decreases as interaction scope expands, indicating information decay consistent with real-world diffusion principles.

isolated_nodes.name: LLM agents exhibit emergent human-like behavior
isolated_nodes.description: By scaling their numbers, LLM-powered agents exhibit the emergence of human-like behaviors at both individual and population levels, motivating simulation of human social behaviors.

isolated_nodes.name: Collaborative filtering inspiration from BPR/NCF
isolated_nodes.description: AgentCF's solution is inspired by the collaborative learning idea from traditional recommendation models such as BPR and NCF, where user and item parameters are collaboratively optimized.

isolated_nodes.name: Task-focused reflection differs from collaborative reflection
isolated_nodes.description: Methods like Reflexion and Self-Refine optimize general-purpose agents through self-learning based on their own exploration, which differs from the collaborative learning emphasized in AgentCF.

isolated_nodes.name: Dataset construction
isolated_nodes.description: Experiments use sampled dense and sparse subsets (100 users each) from Amazon 'CDs and Vinyl' and 'Office Products' review datasets due to expensive API call costs.

isolated_nodes.name: Evaluation protocol
isolated_nodes.description: Performance is evaluated using NDCG@1/5/10 with a leave-one-out strategy, ranking the ground-truth last item alongside nine randomly sampled negative items, averaged over three repetitions.

isolated_nodes.name: Baseline models
isolated_nodes.description: AgentCF is compared against BPR, SASRec, Pop, BM25, and LLMRank as baseline recommendation methods.

isolated_nodes.name: Collaborative advertisement creation
isolated_nodes.description: Multiple advertiser agents proficient in different aspects (personalization, creativity, attractiveness) critique and refine an advertisement draft, producing more appealing advertisements through collaboration, illustrating collective intelligence potential.

structural_reasoning: The graph captures the paper's full argumentative structure: motivation for treating both users and items as agents (C1), the detailed collaborative memory/reflection/propagation method (C2), overall performance results (C3), ablation study components (C4), bias robustness analysis (C5), reflection effectiveness over optimization steps (C6), and three additional interaction-type simulations (user-user C7, item-item C8, and preference propagation C9). These components closely mirror the paper's section structure and exhibit strong internal coherence, particularly the core method component (C2) which traces a clear causal chain from memory design through reflection to preference propagation and the classical-recommender analogy. Ablation findings (C4) are recorded as parallel independent findings without edges since each ablation targets a distinct component rather than forming a causal chain. Background/setup material (motivation for LLM agents generally, dataset/evaluation details, baselines) is appropriately isolated as supporting context.
